title: Washington Returns General Howe's Dog
text:
In the autumn of 1777 the British army under General William Howe captured Philadelphia, the American capital. On October 4 George Washington attacked part of Howe's forces at Germantown, just outside the city. The attack, fought in thick fog, ended in confusion and an American retreat.

Afterward, by tradition, American soldiers found a small dog wandering near the lines. Its collar bore the name of General Howe. Washington ordered it returned to its owner under a flag of truce, with a short note in the handwriting of his aide Alexander Hamilton.

The note survives among Washington's papers, dated October 6, 1777. It reads: "General Washington's compliments to General Howe. He does himself the pleasure to return him a Dog, which accidentally fell into his hands, and by the inscription on the Collar appears to belong to General Howe."

The war went on for six more years. But the two commanders, fighting each other in deadly earnest, had exchanged a moment of plain courtesy, and the note became one of the small, much loved documents of the Revolution.
lesson: Courtesy toward an opponent costs almost nothing and reveals a great deal about your character. You can fight hard and still behave decently.
people: George Washington, William Howe, Alexander Hamilton
source: George Washington to William Howe, October 6, 1777, The Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series, vol. 11
